summary: This document proposed a new document series, IETF Operational Notes, as a repository for operations documents that are more ephemeral than RFCs but more referenceable than Internet-Drafts. It was an experiment under the RFC 3933 process. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6393.

eli5.summary: The IETF wanted a middle shelf for notes: less permanent than books, more official than loose papers. This proposed that shelf as a trial. It is now historic.

questions: how do ionS differ from rfcs
subtitle: A proposal for a middle tier of documents to hold IETF operational procedures.

tldr.problem: The IETF has operational procedures and administrative documents that are too permanent and formal for Internet-Drafts, but too temporary and informal for RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: IETF Operational Notes (IONs) create a new document series with explicit approval by IESG, IAB, or IAOC, versioning, a public archive, and the ability to be updated without the full RFC publication process.
tldr.outcome: This was a 12-month process experiment that was tried and later replaced by RFC 6393, showing the IETF continued to explore how to document its procedures.

today: RFC 4693 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 6393, which made IONs a permanent part of the IETF's documentation infrastructure with the status of Best Current Practice.

sections.title: The Problem with Existing Options
sections.content:
The IETF documents its operational procedures—how to submit an Internet-Draft, how to handle spam on mailing lists, how to run working group meetings—but these fit awkwardly into existing document categories. RFCs are permanent and require a full consensus call and RFC Editor review, making them expensive to update. Internet-Drafts are temporary (expiring after six months) and imply the work is not yet final. Web pages can be changed at will and leave no audit trail.

This RFC proposes IETF Operational Notes (IONs) as a middle ground: more formal than web pages, more updateable than RFCs, and more permanent than Internet-Drafts. An ION has an explicit approval date, a clear approving body, and an archived version history.
sections.eli5: The IETF needed a way to store rules and instructions: not as permanent as a book, not as temporary as a loose note, but somewhere in between.

sections.title: How IONs Work
sections.content:
An ION is a versioned document with a name, a title, an approval date, and an identification of the approving body (IESG, IAB, or IAOC). Unlike RFCs, IONs have no category field—they could cover almost anything from the IETF's operations. The format of an ION is not constrained: it can be plain text, HTML, or any other format the approving body chooses.

When a new ION is issued with the same name, it obsoletes the previous version. The pair of name and approval date forms a stable identifier for a specific version of an ION and never changes, even if the document is later withdrawn. This ensures that historical references remain valid.
sections.eli5: An ION is like a memo: it has a date it was approved, who approved it, and when there is a new version, the old version is marked as outdated.

sections.title: Approval and Authority
sections.content:
IONs are approved by designated bodies: the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group), the IAB (Internet Architecture Board), or the IAOC (IETF Administrative Oversight Committee). Each body can approve IONs in its area of responsibility. A decision by any body other than the IESG can be appealed to the IESG, and IESG decisions can be appealed using the normal IETF appeals process.

An ION approved by IESG, IAB, or IAOC carries the formal authority of that body's statement. However, an ION cannot change the IETF standards process itself, as defined in the BCP (Best Current Practice) series—those are protected by a requirement for explicit IETF consensus.
sections.eli5: When someone in charge approves an ION, it means the organization officially stands behind it. But IONs cannot change the most important rules.

sections.title: Publishing and Archiving IONs
sections.content:
All approved IONs are stored in a public ION Store operated by the IETF secretariat, accessible via HTTP and FTP. The store provides both a way to find the current version of an ION and bulk downloads of all versions for backup and analysis. Draft IONs are published separately and marked with the word 'DRAFT', a publication date, and the body intended to approve them. The repository preserves the version history of draft IONs during the experiment period.

An ION can be published as a draft before approval, but this is not required. The formal approval and archive storage distinguish an ION from an ad-hoc web page.
sections.eli5: IONs are stored in one central place where anyone can find them, and old versions are kept so you can see what changed.

sections.title: The 12-Month Experiment
sections.content:
RFC 4693 proposed IONs as a 12-month process experiment under RFC 3933. After the first ION was published, the IETF would run the series for one year, then issue a community call for feedback on three questions: should the series be made permanent, abandoned, or extended for further study?

The success or failure of the experiment was not to be measured by objective metrics but by the community's view of its usefulness compared to existing options (RFCs, Internet-Drafts, web pages). If the feedback favored keeping the series, the IESG could create a permanent BCP RFC to govern it. If not, the repository would be closed and the ION documents would revert to the status of ordinary web pages.
sections.eli5: This was a trial to see if IONs would help the IETF. After a year, the organization would ask: are IONs useful? Should we keep them?
